criteria: Estimates the area of an irregular shape using a systematic method.
Calculates or estimates the perimeter accurately.
States the precision of the estimate and its limitations.

descriptors.title: Volume and capacity of right prisms
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the volume and capacity of right prisms using appropriate units

nodes.label: Unit relationships between volume and capacity
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand and apply the relationships 1 cm³ = 1 mL, 1000 cm³ = 1 L, 1 m³ = 1000 L, and use these to convert between volume and capacity units.
criteria: Correctly converts between cm³, mL, L and m³.
Selects appropriate units for a given practical context.
Does not confuse cm³ and cm (volume vs length).

nodes.label: Solving practical volume and capacity problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve practical problems involving volume and capacity of right prisms, including optimisation and multi-step contexts.
criteria: Selects and applies the correct formula for the prism type.
Interprets the result in context with appropriate units.
Identifies which measurements are relevant to the problem.

descriptors.title: Circumference and area of circles
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the circumference and area of a circle using formulas and appropriate units

nodes.label: Deriving the area of a circle formula
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand why A = πr² using at least one informal derivation method.
criteria: States A = πr² and can explain the formula using at least one informal argument.
Explains why the area must be between 2r² and 4r².
Does not confuse area formula with circumference formula.

nodes.label: Applying circle area and circumference formulas
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply A = πr² and C = 2πr to calculate area and circumference, find radius/diameter given area or circumference, and solve composite shape problems.
criteria: Correctly calculates area given radius or radius given area.
Solves a composite shape problem involving circular components.
Uses an appropriate approximation for π and states it.

descriptors.title: Duration and time zones
descriptors.description: solve problems involving duration, including using 12- and 24-hour time across multiple time zones

nodes.label: Converting between time zones
nodes.checkpoint: Students convert times between time zones using UTC offsets and apply 12- and 24-hour time conventions.
criteria: Correctly converts a time between two given time zones.
Handles day changes correctly when conversion crosses midnight.
Uses 24-hour time appropriately to avoid AM/PM ambiguity.

nodes.label: Solving multi-zone scheduling and itinerary problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve practical problems involving scheduling across multiple time zones, including travel itineraries and virtual meeting planning.
criteria: Correctly plans a meeting or itinerary accounting for all time zone offsets.
Identifies and resolves day-change issues.
Communicates the solution clearly showing local times in each zone.

descriptors.title: Rates
descriptors.description: recognise and use rates to solve problems involving the comparison of 2 related quantities of different units of measure

nodes.label: Rates as comparisons of different units
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise that a rate compares two quantities with different units and express rates in standard form (quantity per unit).
criteria: Correctly identifies and writes a rate from a practical context.
Converts between related rate units.
Distinguishes a rate (different units) from a ratio (same units).

nodes.label: Applying rates to practical problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply rates to solve practical problems including pay rates, run rates, dilution, taxation, and unit conversions.
criteria: Correctly applies a given rate to solve a practical problem.
Shows the rate calculation clearly with appropriate units.
Interprets the result in context.

descriptors.title: Pythagoras' theorem
descriptors.description: use Pythagoras' theorem to solve problems involving the side lengths of right-angled triangles

nodes.label: Understanding and stating Pythagoras' theorem
nodes.checkpoint: Students state Pythagoras' theorem (a² + b² = c²) and understand it as a relationship between areas of squares on the sides of a right-angled triangle.
criteria: States Pythagoras' theorem correctly and identifies the hypotenuse.
Verifies the theorem for at least one specific case.
States the converse: if a² + b² = c² then the triangle is right-angled.

nodes.label: Finding unknown side lengths using Pythagoras
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply Pythagoras' theorem to find the hypotenuse or a shorter side in right-angled triangles, including in practical and coordinate geometry contexts.
criteria: Correctly identifies the hypotenuse in a given right-angled triangle.
Finds an unknown side correctly using the theorem.
Applies the theorem to a practical problem context.

nodes.label: Classifying triangles using side lengths
nodes.checkpoint: Students use the relationship between a² + b² and c² to classify triangles as right-angled, acute or obtuse.
criteria: Correctly classifies a triangle given three side lengths.
States the rule for each classification (right, acute, obtuse).
Identifies the longest side as c before applying the test.

descriptors.title: Modelling with ratios and rates
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving ratios and rates, including financial contexts; formulate problems; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, reviewing the appropriateness of the model

nodes.label: Formulating and solving ratio/rate models
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify whether a problem requires a ratio or rate model, formulate it, and solve in context.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether the problem requires a ratio or rate model.
Formulates and solves the model correctly.
Justifies the model choice and interprets the solution in context.

nodes.label: Reviewing model appropriateness
nodes.checkpoint: Students evaluate whether a ratio or rate model is appropriate for a given situation, identify assumptions, and suggest improvements.
criteria: Identifies at least one assumption made in a given model.
Explains how the assumption affects the model's accuracy.
Suggests a reasonable refinement to the model.

descriptors.title: Irrational numbers
descriptors.description: recognise irrational numbers in applied contexts, including square roots and π

nodes.label: Irrational numbers as non-terminating, non-recurring decimals
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that irrational numbers cannot be expressed as fractions and have decimal expansions that neither terminate nor recur.
criteria: States that irrational numbers cannot be expressed as fractions and have non-terminating non-recurring decimal expansions.
Correctly classifies given numbers as rational or irrational.
Does not confuse 'irrational' with 'very large' or 'impossible to use in calculation'.

nodes.label: Locating irrational numbers on the real number line
nodes.checkpoint: Students approximately locate irrational numbers on the real number line and understand the real number system as including both rational and irrational numbers.
criteria: Correctly locates an irrational number between two consecutive integers on the number line.
Describes the real number system as including both rationals and irrationals.
Does not treat the decimal approximation as the exact value.

descriptors.title: Exponent laws
descriptors.description: establish and apply the exponent laws with positive integer exponents and the zero-exponent, using exponent notation with numbers

nodes.label: Establishing the exponent laws from expanded form
nodes.checkpoint: Students derive the product of powers, quotient of powers, and power of a power rules from expanded form, and state each rule.
criteria: Derives at least one exponent law from expanded form.
States all three laws and the zero exponent correctly.
Explains why a⁰ = 1.

nodes.label: Applying exponent laws in combination
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply the exponent laws individually and in combination to simplify numerical expressions, checking that bases are the same before applying.
criteria: Correctly applies each exponent law individually.
Applies laws in combination without confusing different-base expressions.
Does not apply exponent laws when bases differ.

descriptors.title: Terminating and recurring decimals
descriptors.description: recognise terminating and recurring decimals, using digital tools as appropriate

nodes.label: Identifying terminating and recurring decimals
nodes.checkpoint: Students distinguish terminating from recurring decimals and use correct notation for recurring decimals.
criteria: Correctly classifies a fraction's decimal expansion as terminating or recurring.
Writes a recurring decimal using correct notation.
Does not confuse recurring with irrational (non-terminating, non-recurring).

nodes.label: Predicting termination from prime factorisation of denominator
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify whether a fraction terminates by examining whether the prime factorisation of the denominator contains only factors of 2 and/or 5.
criteria: Correctly predicts whether a fraction terminates from its denominator's prime factorisation.
Explains why the rule works (connection to base 10).
Simplifies fractions first where necessary before applying the rule.

descriptors.title: Four operations with integers
descriptors.description: use the 4 operations with integers and with rational numbers, choosing and using efficient strategies and digital tools where appropriate

nodes.label: Multiplication and division of integers
nodes.checkpoint: Students establish and apply the sign rules for multiplication and division of integers, including negative × negative = positive.
criteria: Correctly applies sign rules for all combinations of integer multiplication and division.
Explains the sign rule for negative × negative.
Does not confuse multiplication sign rules with addition sign rules.

nodes.label: Efficient strategies for rational number operations
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply all four operations to rational numbers including negative fractions and decimals, selecting efficient strategies and digital tools appropriately.
criteria: Correctly computes with negative fractions and decimals.
Selects an efficient strategy and can justify why.
Does not default to the most laborious method when a simpler one is available.

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling with percentages
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving rational numbers and percentages, including financial contexts; formulate problems, choosing efficient calculation strategies and using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, reviewing the appropriateness of the model

nodes.label: Modelling percentage increase and decrease
nodes.checkpoint: Students model situations involving percentage increase and decrease, including mark-ups, discounts, and GST, and explain why the result is an increase or decrease.
criteria: Correctly models a percentage increase or decrease problem.
Explains why the change is an increase or decrease.
Uses an efficient multiplier strategy where appropriate.

nodes.label: Modelling financial and real-world contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students formulate and solve models for financial problems including personal income tax, and interpret and communicate solutions including review of model appropriateness.
criteria: Formulates a model correctly from a financial or real-world context.
Interprets the solution with appropriate units and contextual meaning.
Reviews whether the model captures the situation accurately.

descriptors.title: Complementary events
descriptors.description: recognise that complementary events have a combined probability of one; use this relationship to calculate probabilities in applied contexts

nodes.label: Recognising complementary events
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise complementary events as pairs that together cover all outcomes, and state that P(A) + P(not A) = 1.
criteria: Correctly identifies the complement of a given event.
States P(A) + P(not A) = 1 and verifies it for a specific case.
Does not confuse complementary events with mutually exclusive events.

nodes.label: Using the complement relationship to calculate probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students use P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to calculate probabilities in applied contexts, including cases where finding the complement is more efficient than direct calculation.
criteria: Correctly calculates P(not A) given P(A) and vice versa.
Identifies at least one context where finding the complement is more efficient.
Applies the complement relationship correctly to a practical problem.

descriptors.title: Combinations for two events
descriptors.description: determine all possible combinations for 2 events, using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, and use these to determine probabilities of specific outcomes in practical situations

nodes.label: Representing two-event combinations
nodes.checkpoint: Students represent all possible combinations for two events using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams.
criteria: Correctly lists all combinations for a two-event situation.
Represents combinations accurately using at least one method.
Identifies the advantage of each representation for different questions.

nodes.label: Calculating compound event probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students use representations to calculate probabilities of compound events using 'and', 'or' (inclusive and exclusive), and 'at least' language.
criteria: Correctly calculates P(A and B) and P(A or B) from a representation.
Distinguishes inclusive and exclusive 'or' in context.
Uses the representation systematically rather than guessing.

descriptors.title: Simulations of compound events
descriptors.description: conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations, using digital tools to determine probabilities for compound events, and describe results

nodes.label: Setting up and running compound event simulations
nodes.checkpoint: Students use digital simulation tools to simulate two-event compound scenarios and record results systematically.
criteria: Sets up and runs a digital simulation for a compound event.
Records results in an organised frequency table.
Selects an appropriate number of trials for the simulation.

nodes.label: Using simulation results to determine and describe probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students compare simulated relative frequencies to theoretical probabilities for compound events and describe what the results reveal.
criteria: Calculates relative frequency from simulation results correctly.
Compares observed relative frequency to theoretical probability.
Explains discrepancies using the concept of sampling variation.

descriptors.title: Congruence and similarity
descriptors.description: identify the conditions for congruence and similarity of triangles and explain the conditions for other sets of common shapes to be congruent or similar, including those formed by transformations

nodes.label: Congruence conditions for triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify and apply the four conditions for triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS) and explain why each is sufficient.
criteria: States all four congruence conditions correctly.
Identifies which condition applies to a given pair of triangles.
Explains why SSA is not a valid congruence condition.

nodes.label: Similarity conditions for triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify and apply the conditions for triangle similarity (AA, SAS, SSS) and understand similarity as a scaled version of congruence.
criteria: Identifies similar triangles and states the condition used.
Correctly calculates a missing side using the scale factor.
Maintains consistent matching of corresponding sides.

nodes.label: Congruence and similarity in other shapes and transformations
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain the conditions for congruence and similarity in other common shapes and connect congruence to transformations.
criteria: States conditions for congruence and similarity for a given shape type.
Connects congruence to rigid transformations and similarity to enlargement.
Correctly identifies whether two given shapes are congruent, similar, or neither.

descriptors.title: Properties of quadrilaterals
descriptors.description: establish properties of quadrilaterals using congruent triangles and angle properties, and solve related problems explaining reasoning

nodes.label: Establishing quadrilateral properties via congruent triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students use diagonal decomposition into triangles and congruence arguments to establish properties of specific quadrilaterals.
criteria: Uses a congruence argument to establish at least one quadrilateral property.
States each step with a geometric reason.
Does not assert properties without justification.

nodes.label: Solving problems using quadrilateral properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students use established quadrilateral properties to find unknown angles and lengths, providing full geometric reasoning.
criteria: Finds unknown angles or lengths using quadrilateral properties correctly.
States a geometric reason for each step.
Solves at least one multi-step problem without prompting for each step.

descriptors.title: 3D coordinate systems
descriptors.description: describe the position and location of objects in 3 dimensions in different ways, including using a three-dimensional coordinate system with the use of dynamic geometric software and other digital tools

nodes.label: Extending the coordinate system to three dimensions
nodes.checkpoint: Students extend the 2D Cartesian plane to three dimensions by adding a third axis (z), and plot and read coordinates in the first octant.
criteria: Plots a point given 3D coordinates in the first octant.
Reads the coordinates of a plotted point.
Identifies which axis extends the 2D plane to 3D.

nodes.label: Describing positions in real-world 3D systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students describe positions in practical 3D reference systems including latitude/longitude/altitude and multi-storey coordinate systems.
criteria: Correctly describes a position using a practical 3D reference system.
Interprets a 3D coordinate in a real-world context.
Connects the three coordinates to three independent dimensions of location.

descriptors.title: Algorithms for congruence and similarity
descriptors.description: design, create and test algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions that identify congruency or similarity of shapes, and describe how the algorithm works

nodes.label: Designing a congruence/similarity classification algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students design a step-by-step algorithm that correctly classifies two triangles as congruent, similar, or neither, using the appropriate conditions.
criteria: Designs an algorithm that correctly classifies triangles using at least two conditions.
Includes clear decision points with yes/no branches.
Tests the algorithm with at least two examples and corrects any errors.

nodes.label: Evaluating and describing algorithms
nodes.checkpoint: Students trace through a given algorithm with test cases, identify errors or limitations, and describe in plain language how it works.
criteria: Correctly traces an algorithm with given inputs.
Identifies at least one error or limitation in a given algorithm.
Describes the algorithm's logic in plain language.

descriptors.title: Data collection techniques
descriptors.description: investigate techniques for data collection including census, sampling, experiment and observation, and explain the practicalities and implications of obtaining data through these techniques

nodes.label: Census vs sampling and collection technique selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students distinguish census from sampling and identify when each is appropriate; describe the main data collection techniques.
criteria: Correctly distinguishes census from sampling.
Identifies an appropriate collection technique for a given context and justifies the choice.
Explains at least one practical limitation of sampling.

nodes.label: Bias in data collection
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise and explain sources of bias in data collection and describe how bias affects conclusions.
criteria: Identifies a source of bias in a data collection scenario.
Explains the likely direction and effect of the bias.
Suggests a concrete method to reduce the identified bias.

descriptors.title: Sampling methods and distribution analysis
descriptors.description: analyse and report on the distribution of data from primary and secondary sources using random and non-random sampling techniques to select and study samples

nodes.label: Comparing sampling methods
nodes.checkpoint: Students compare simple random, systematic, stratified and convenience sampling methods and evaluate the reliability of each.
criteria: Describes at least three different sampling methods.
Explains the reliability advantage of random over convenience sampling.
Selects and justifies an appropriate sampling method for a given context.

nodes.label: Analysing and reporting on sample distributions
nodes.checkpoint: Students collect or obtain a sample, analyse the distribution, and report findings from primary or secondary sources.
criteria: Collects or obtains a sample using a valid method.
Analyses and describes the distribution appropriately.
Comments on how the sampling method may have affected the distribution.

descriptors.title: Sample size and variation
descriptors.description: compare variations in distributions and proportions obtained from random samples of the same size drawn from a population and recognise the effect of sample size on this variation

nodes.label: Sampling variation — same population, different samples
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise that samples from the same population produce different distributions due to chance, and describe the range of variation.
criteria: Explains that samples from the same population will naturally vary.
Describes the range of variation observed across multiple samples.
Does not conclude that sampling variation means the data is wrong.

nodes.label: Effect of sample size on variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students investigate and describe how increasing sample size reduces variation in sample statistics, and apply this to making inferences.
criteria: States that larger samples produce less variation in statistics.
Demonstrates the relationship using simulation data.
Applies the principle to justify a recommendation about sample size in a practical context.

descriptors.title: Statistical investigations with samples
descriptors.description: plan and conduct statistical investigations involving samples of a population; use ethical and fair methods to make inferences about the population and report findings, acknowledging uncertainty

nodes.label: Planning an ethical investigation with sampling
nodes.checkpoint: Students plan a statistical investigation including ethical and fair sampling methods, anticipate sources of uncertainty, and identify how findings will be used to make inferences.
criteria: Specifies the population, sample, and sampling method.
Identifies at least one ethical consideration and addresses it in the plan.
States what inference will be drawn from the investigation.

nodes.label: Conducting, inferring and reporting with uncertainty
nodes.checkpoint: Students conduct the investigation, make inferences about the population from the sample, and report findings while explicitly acknowledging the uncertainty introduced by sampling.
criteria: Makes a valid inference about the population from the sample.
Explicitly acknowledges uncertainty in the report.
Connects the degree of uncertainty to the sample size and method.

descriptors.title: Exponent laws
descriptors.description: apply the exponent laws to numerical expressions with integer exponents and extend to variables

nodes.label: Negative integer exponents
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate expressions with negative integer exponents and explain why a negative exponent produces a reciprocal.
criteria: Correctly evaluates at least two expressions with negative integer exponents as fractions
Explains using a pattern or sequence why a negative exponent produces a reciprocal
Does not confuse a negative exponent with a negative result

nodes.label: Exponent laws with numerical expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply all exponent laws (product, quotient, power of a power, power of a product, zero exponent) to simplify numerical expressions with integer exponents and explain why each law works.
criteria: Correctly names and applies at least three distinct exponent laws to simplify a multi-step numerical expression
Justifies at least one step using first-principles counting of factors
Correctly handles the zero exponent (any non-zero base to the power 0 equals 1)

nodes.label: Extending exponent laws to variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply exponent laws to simplify algebraic expressions involving variables, including products, quotients and powers of expressions with constants and variables.
criteria: Correctly simplifies at least two algebraic expressions involving exponent laws, including one with multiple variables
Applies the convention x⁰=1 and x¹=x correctly
Uses negative exponents correctly in algebraic expressions (e.g. writes 1/x² as x⁻²)

descriptors.title: Binomial products and factorisation
descriptors.description: simplify algebraic expressions, expand binomial products and factorise monic quadratic expressions

nodes.label: Expanding binomial products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can expand a product of two linear binomials using the distributive property and simplify the result.
criteria: Correctly expands (x+a)(x+b) for integer a and b, including when one or both are negative
Shows all four partial products before collecting like terms
Correctly simplifies the middle term (a+b)x by combining the two linear partial products

nodes.label: Generalising the expansion pattern
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the pattern (x+a)(x+b) = x²+(a+b)x+ab and use it to expand binomial products and predict features of the result.
criteria: States the general pattern (x+a)(x+b) = x²+(a+b)x+ab correctly
Correctly predicts the constant term and the coefficient of x for a new binomial product before expanding
Identifies at least one expansion where the middle term cancels (difference of squares)

nodes.label: Factorising monic quadratics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can factorise monic quadratic expressions x²+bx+c with integer roots by finding two integers whose product is c and sum is b.
criteria: Correctly identifies the factor pair (two integers with the correct product and sum) for a monic quadratic
Writes the factorised form correctly as (x+p)(x+q)
Verifies the factorisation by expanding and recovering the original expression

nodes.label: Expansion and factorisation as inverse operations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can move fluently between expanded and factorised forms of monic quadratics and explain the relationship between the two operations.
criteria: Correctly factorises a monic quadratic and verifies by expansion
Explains the inverse relationship between expanding and factorising in their own words
Identifies the correct form (expanded or factorised) to use for a given purpose (e.g. factorised to find roots, expanded to add expressions)

descriptors.title: Gradient, midpoint and distance
descriptors.description: find the gradient of a line segment, the midpoint of the line interval and the distance between 2 distinct points on the Cartesian plane

nodes.label: Gradient from two points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the gradient of a line segment between two given points and explain why gradient is independent of which two points on the line are chosen.
criteria: Correctly calculates gradient (including sign) between two coordinate pairs
Verifies with a third point that gradient is constant along a line
Correctly identifies whether a gradient is positive, negative, zero or undefined from the coordinates

nodes.label: Parallel and perpendicular lines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use gradient to determine whether two lines are parallel or perpendicular.
criteria: Correctly identifies parallel lines by comparing gradients
Correctly calculates the gradient of a line perpendicular to a given line
Verifies the perpendicular relationship using the product m₁×m₂=−1

nodes.label: Distance between two points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the distance between two points on the Cartesian plane using Pythagoras' theorem.
criteria: Correctly identifies the horizontal and vertical distances between two points as the legs of a right triangle
Applies Pythagoras' theorem to calculate the exact distance
Expresses the distance in simplified surd form where appropriate

nodes.label: Midpoint of a line interval
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the midpoint of a line interval between two given points.
criteria: Correctly calculates the midpoint coordinates by averaging x and y values
Verifies the midpoint by confirming it lies equidistant from each endpoint
Applies the midpoint calculation correctly when coordinates are negative or fractional

nodes.label: Applying coordinate geometry in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply gradient, midpoint and distance in combination to solve problems in context, including interpreting gradient as rate of change.
criteria: Correctly selects and applies at least two coordinate geometry tools to solve a contextual problem
Interprets the calculated values (gradient, distance, midpoint) correctly in the context of the problem
Shows clearly labelled working and uses appropriate units or notation

descriptors.title: Quadratic functions and equations
descriptors.description: identify and graph quadratic functions, solve quadratic equations graphically and numerically, and solve monic quadratic equations with integer roots algebraically, using graphing software and digital tools as appropriate

nodes.label: Identifying quadratic relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify quadratic functions from tables of values (using second differences) and from the form of an equation.
criteria: Correctly calculates first and second differences for a given table of values
Correctly identifies a quadratic relationship when second differences are constant
Correctly classifies at least three function equations as quadratic or non-quadratic

nodes.label: Graphing quadratic functions and identifying key features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can graph quadratic functions and identify their key features: turning point, axis of symmetry, x-intercepts, y-intercept, and whether the function has a maximum or minimum.
criteria: Correctly identifies the turning point coordinates and axis of symmetry equation for a graphed quadratic
Correctly reads x-intercepts from the graph and states 'no real solutions' when the graph does not cross the x-axis
Identifies whether the turning point is a maximum or minimum and explains why based on the direction the parabola opens

nodes.label: Solving quadratic equations algebraically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve monic quadratic equations with integer roots algebraically using factorisation and the null factor law.
criteria: Rewrites the equation in the form (x+p)(x+q)=0 before applying the null factor law
Correctly identifies both roots (including cases where roots are zero, equal, or negative)
Verifies at least one solution by substitution back into the original equation

nodes.label: Connecting algebraic, graphical and numerical solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve quadratic equations using multiple methods and explain the connections between graphical x-intercepts, factorised form roots, and numerical solutions.
criteria: Correctly identifies x-intercepts of a quadratic graph and states these as roots of the equation
Explains why a graph with no x-intercepts means the equation has no real solutions
Solves the same quadratic equation using at least two different methods and verifies agreement

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling — change
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve applied problems involving change including financial contexts; formulate problems, choosing to use either linear or quadratic functions; interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate the model and report methods and findings

nodes.label: Formulating a model — choosing function type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a situation involving change is better modelled by a linear or quadratic function and justify the choice.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether the rate of change in the context is constant or non-constant
States and justifies the choice of linear or quadratic model with reference to the context
Formulates the mathematical relationship (table, graph or rule) from the given information

nodes.label: Solving and interpreting the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a mathematical model (linear or quadratic) and interpret the solution in the context of the original problem.
criteria: States the solution with correct units and in the language of the original context
Checks the solution for contextual reasonableness (e.g. positive time, valid domain)
Correctly interprets at least one graphical feature (turning point, intercept) in terms of the situation

nodes.label: Evaluating the model and reporting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the limitations of a mathematical model and report their methods and findings clearly.
criteria: Identifies at least one assumption the model makes and explains what happens if it is violated
States the domain over which the model gives reasonable predictions
Reports the method and conclusion in a way that someone unfamiliar with the problem could follow

descriptors.title: Parameter variation and function families
descriptors.description: experiment with the effects of the variation of parameters on graphs of related functions, using digital tools, making connections between graphical and algebraic representations, and generalising emerging patterns

nodes.label: Parameter variation in linear functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effect of varying the parameters a and b in y=ax+b on the graph, and explain what each parameter controls.
criteria: Correctly describes the effect of increasing or decreasing a on the steepness and direction of the line
Correctly describes the effect of increasing or decreasing b as a vertical shift
States a generalisation about what each parameter controls

nodes.label: Parameter variation in quadratic functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effect of varying the parameters in y=a(x−h)²+k on the graph, and explain how each parameter produces a specific transformation.
criteria: Correctly identifies the turning point (h, k) from the completed square form
Correctly predicts the direction of horizontal translation for y=(x−h)² (shift right when h>0)
States the effect of a negative value of a (reflection in the x-axis) with a correct example

nodes.label: Generalising across function families
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply parameter variation to at least one additional function family (reciprocal, square root, cube or exponential) and identify patterns that generalise across families.
criteria: Correctly describes the effect of at least one transformation on a function family beyond linear/quadratic
Identifies at least one transformation pattern that appears in two or more different function families
States a generalisation (e.g. 'multiplying by a constant stretches the graph vertically in every family I tested')

descriptors.title: Volume and surface area
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the volume and surface area of right prisms and cylinders using appropriate units

nodes.label: Surface area from nets
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the surface area of a right prism or cylinder by identifying and summing the areas of all faces.
criteria: Correctly identifies all faces of a right prism or cylinder and their dimensions
Calculates the area of each face and sums to give total surface area
Uses appropriate units (cm², m²) and maintains consistency throughout

nodes.label: Volume of right prisms and cylinders
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the volume of right prisms and cylinders using V = Ah (cross-sectional area × height).
criteria: Correctly identifies the cross-sectional area as the base of the V=Ah formula
Calculates volume correctly for both right prisms and cylinders
Uses appropriate units (cm³, m³, L) and converts between them where required

nodes.label: Solving problems with surface area and volume
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply surface area and volume calculations to solve practical problems, including selecting the appropriate measure for the context.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether a problem requires surface area or volume and explains why
Solves the problem using the correct formula with appropriate units
Checks that the answer is reasonable in the context of the problem

descriptors.title: Scientific notation
descriptors.description: solve problems involving very small and very large measurements, time scales and intervals expressed in scientific notation

nodes.label: Converting to and from scientific notation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert numbers between decimal form and scientific notation in both directions.
criteria: Correctly converts at least two large numbers and two small numbers to scientific notation
Correctly converts at least two scientific notation values back to decimal form
Uses a coefficient between 1 and 10 in every scientific notation expression

nodes.label: Calculating with scientific notation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform calculations involving numbers expressed in scientific notation by applying exponent laws.
criteria: Correctly multiplies two numbers in scientific notation by multiplying coefficients and adding exponents
Correctly divides two numbers in scientific notation by dividing coefficients and subtracting exponents
Adjusts the result to ensure the coefficient is between 1 and 10 where required

nodes.label: Applying scientific notation in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use scientific notation to solve problems involving very large or very small measurements and time scales.
criteria: Correctly selects and applies scientific notation operations to solve an applied problem
States the answer in scientific notation with appropriate units
Interprets the result meaningfully in the context of the problem (e.g. explains what the order of magnitude means)

descriptors.title: Spatial problems — pythagoras, trig and similarity
descriptors.description: solve spatial problems, applying angle properties, scale, similarity, Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry in right-angled triangles

nodes.label: Trigonometric ratios — finding unknown sides
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply sine, cosine and tangent ratios to find unknown sides in right-angled triangles.
criteria: Correctly labels opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to a specified angle
Selects the correct trigonometric ratio for the given information
Calculates the unknown side correctly to an appropriate number of decimal places

nodes.label: Trigonometric ratios — finding unknown angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply inverse trigonometric ratios to find unknown angles in right-angled triangles.
criteria: Correctly sets up the trigonometric ratio from two known sides
Applies the inverse trigonometric function to find the angle
States the angle in degrees with appropriate precision

nodes.label: Similarity, scale and proportion in triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply similarity and scale factor to solve problems involving corresponding sides and areas of similar triangles.
criteria: Correctly identifies corresponding sides in similar triangles and the scale factor
Correctly applies the scale factor to find an unknown side
Correctly applies k² (not k) when finding the ratio of areas of similar figures

nodes.label: Solving multi-concept spatial problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve spatial problems requiring a combination of Pythagoras' theorem, trigonometry, similarity and/or scale.
criteria: Draws a labelled diagram identifying all known and unknown quantities
Selects and applies at least two appropriate tools in the correct sequence
States the solution with appropriate units and precision

descriptors.title: Measurement error
descriptors.description: calculate and interpret absolute, relative and percentage errors in measurements, recognising that all measurements are estimates

nodes.label: All measurements are estimates
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why all measurements are estimates and identify lower and upper bounds for a given measurement.
criteria: States that all measurements are estimates and gives a reason related to instrument precision or reading
Correctly calculates lower and upper bounds for a measurement given its precision
Identifies the half-unit uncertainty corresponding to the precision of a given instrument

nodes.label: Absolute and relative error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate and distinguish absolute error and relative error for a measurement.
criteria: Correctly calculates absolute error as |measured value − exact value|
Correctly calculates relative error as absolute error ÷ exact value
Explains in their own words why relative error allows comparison across different scales

nodes.label: Percentage error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate and interpret percentage error, using absolute value where appropriate.
criteria: Correctly calculates percentage error using the formula (|measured − exact| / exact) × 100
States the percentage error with % units and explains what it means
Identifies at least one context where using absolute value in the formula is important

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling — proportion, rates and ratio
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving direct proportion, rates, ratio and scale, including financial contexts; formulate the problems and interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate the model and report methods and findings

nodes.label: Identifying and formulating proportion and rate relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a situation involves direct proportion or a rate, represent it mathematically, and formulate it as a model.
criteria: Correctly identifies the constant of proportionality and writes the mathematical relationship
Defines variables clearly and states units
Represents the relationship in at least one form (equation, table or graph)

nodes.label: Solving and interpreting the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a proportion or rate model and interpret the solution in the context of the original problem.
criteria: Correctly solves the proportion or rate equation
States the solution with units in the language of the original context
Checks whether the solution is contextually reasonable

nodes.label: Evaluating and reporting the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the limitations of a proportion or rate model and report methods and findings.
criteria: States at least one assumption underlying the proportion model
Identifies a context or domain boundary where the model would not apply
Reports the method and conclusion clearly enough for someone unfamiliar with the problem to follow

descriptors.title: Real number system
descriptors.description: recognise that the real number system includes the rational numbers and the irrational numbers, and solve problems involving real numbers using digital tools

nodes.label: Subsets of the real number system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the hierarchy of number subsets — natural numbers, integers, rationals, irrationals — and explain what distinguishes each from the others.
criteria: Correctly classifies at least four different numbers into the appropriate subsets of the real number system
Explains the distinguishing property of rational numbers (expressible as p/q for integers p, q, q≠0) in their own words
Identifies that integers are rational, not a separate category outside rationals

nodes.label: Exact and approximate representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between exact representations of irrational numbers (e.g. √2, π) and their decimal approximations, and explain why decimal approximations are not equal to the exact value.
criteria: Correctly identifies a given decimal value as an approximation of an irrational and states which irrational it approximates
Explains why no finite decimal expansion can exactly equal an irrational number
Writes an exact form (e.g. √3) and a correct decimal approximation for the same value, labelling which is which

nodes.label: Real number line and inequalities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate real numbers (including irrationals) on the number line and represent solution intervals for linear inequalities.
criteria: Correctly locates at least two irrational numbers approximately on a number line relative to known values
Solves a linear inequality and represents the solution interval correctly on a number line
Uses correct inequality notation and open/closed circle conventions when marking solution intervals

nodes.label: Solving problems with real numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve problems by substituting real numbers (including irrationals) into formulas, expressing solutions in both exact and approximate decimal form as appropriate.
criteria: Correctly substitutes real number values into a formula and simplifies
Expresses the answer in exact form where appropriate (e.g. 9π cm²) and as a decimal approximation correct to 2 decimal places
Uses correct units and explains the choice between exact and approximate form

descriptors.title: Compound events
descriptors.description: list all outcomes for compound events both with and without replacement, using lists, tree diagrams, tables or arrays; assign probabilities to outcomes

nodes.label: Systematic listing of compound event outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can list all outcomes for a two-step compound event using a systematic method (list, tree diagram, table or array).
criteria: Lists all outcomes using a systematic method (tree diagram, table or array)
Verifies completeness by confirming the count matches the expected number of outcomes
Represents the outcome space clearly with no duplicates or omissions

nodes.label: With and without replacement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how replacing or not replacing changes the sample space and the probabilities assigned to outcomes.
criteria: Correctly adjusts the sample space and branch probabilities when replacement is removed
Explains why without-replacement probabilities change at each stage
Correctly assigns probabilities to at least three outcomes in a without-replacement tree diagram

nodes.label: Assigning probabilities to compound event outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can assign probabilities to all outcomes of a compound event and verify that probabilities sum to 1.
criteria: Assigns correct probabilities to all outcomes of a compound event
Multiplies probabilities along branches correctly to find the probability of a specific compound outcome
Verifies that all outcome probabilities sum to 1

descriptors.title: Relative frequencies and compound probability
descriptors.description: calculate relative frequencies from given or collected data to estimate probabilities of events involving "and", inclusive "or" and exclusive "or"

nodes.label: Relative frequency as a probability estimate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate relative frequencies from data and explain how they estimate theoretical probability for compound events.
criteria: Correctly calculates relative frequency as (number of times event occurred) ÷ (total number of trials)
States that larger samples give more reliable relative frequency estimates
Uses a relative frequency to make a probability estimate for a future event

nodes.label: Compound events: 'and', inclusive 'or', exclusive 'or'
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between 'and', inclusive 'or' and exclusive 'or' events and represent them using Venn diagrams or two-way tables.
criteria: Correctly distinguishes inclusive 'or' (A ∪ B) from exclusive 'or' (A or B but not both) on a Venn diagram
Correctly identifies the region for 'A and B' (intersection) on a Venn diagram
Calculates the correct frequency/probability for each compound event type from a given data set

nodes.label: Estimating compound event probabilities from data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use relative frequencies from data to estimate probabilities of compound events ('and', 'or') and use these to make predictions.
criteria: Correctly calculates relative frequencies for both 'and' and 'or' compound events from the same data set
Uses a Venn diagram or two-way table to organise the data before calculating
Makes a reasonable prediction based on the estimated probability and explains the reasoning

descriptors.title: Chance experiments and simulations
descriptors.description: design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations, using digital tools to compare probabilities of simple events to related compound events, and describe results

nodes.label: Designing a chance experiment or simulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a chance experiment or simulation that will generate data to compare the probability of a simple event to a related compound event.
criteria: Specifies the outcome space, what is recorded, and the number of trials
Correctly models the probability structure (with/without replacement, equal/unequal probabilities)
Explains how the simulation replicates the real event

nodes.label: Conducting the experiment and comparing probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can conduct a repeated chance experiment or simulation using digital tools, compare results for simple and compound events, and describe results.
criteria: Conducts the simulation with a sufficient number of trials (at least 50) using a digital tool
Correctly calculates relative frequencies for both the simple and compound events
Compares the two results and describes what the comparison reveals

nodes.label: Describing and evaluating results
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe simulation results, compare experimental to theoretical probabilities, and explain any discrepancies.
criteria: States the experimental probability and the corresponding theoretical probability
Explains why the two values are unlikely to be identical for a finite number of trials
Identifies what aspect of the design or trial count could be changed to reduce the discrepancy

descriptors.title: Trigonometric ratios
descriptors.description: recognise the constancy of the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for a given angle in right-angled triangles using properties of similarity

nodes.label: Sides of a right-angled triangle relative to an angle
nodes.checkpoint: Students can correctly identify the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides for a specified angle in a right-angled triangle.
criteria: Correctly labels hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent for a specified angle in at least three different triangle orientations
Explains that opposite and adjacent are defined relative to the angle, not absolute positions
Correctly re-labels when the specified angle changes within the same triangle

nodes.label: Constancy of ratios — similarity argument
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain using properties of similarity why the ratio of two specified sides is constant for a given angle, regardless of triangle size.
criteria: Calculates the same ratio (e.g. opposite/hypotenuse) for at least two similar triangles with the same angle and shows the values are equal
Explains why the ratio is constant using the property of similar triangles
Confirms that the ratio changes when a different angle is used

nodes.label: Naming the ratios: sine, cosine, tangent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the sine, cosine and tangent ratios and connect each to the appropriate pair of sides in a right-angled triangle.
criteria: States the correct ratio definition for each of sin, cos and tan
Correctly evaluates each ratio for a right-angled triangle with given side lengths
Correctly connects the tangent ratio to the gradient of a line

descriptors.title: Enlargement transformation
descriptors.description: apply the enlargement transformation to shapes and objects using dynamic geometry software as appropriate; identify and explain aspects that remain the same and those that change

nodes.label: Invariant and changing properties under enlargement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify which properties of a shape are preserved under enlargement (angles, shape) and which change (side lengths, perimeter, area).
criteria: Correctly applies enlargement transformation and identifies the image dimensions
Lists at least two properties that are invariant (angles, shape) and two that change (lengths, area)
Uses the scale factor correctly to calculate new dimensions

nodes.label: Scale factor relationships for length, area and volume
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generalise the relationships between scale factor k and the scaling of length (×k), area (×k²) and volume (×k³).
criteria: States and applies the correct scaling relationships: lengths ×k, areas ×k², volumes ×k³
Verifies the area scaling relationship (×k²) for at least two different scale factors
Explains in their own words why area scales as k² (two dimensions each scaled by k)

descriptors.title: Geometric algorithms
descriptors.description: design, test and refine algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions based on geometric constructions and theorems; discuss and evaluate refinements

nodes.label: Representing a geometric process as an algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a known geometric construction or theorem application as a step-by-step algorithm using pseudocode or a flowchart.
criteria: Writes a step-by-step algorithm with clear, unambiguous steps
Correctly identifies at least one decision step (with two branches) and at least one computation step
Uses pseudocode or flowchart notation consistently

nodes.label: Testing an algorithm with cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can test an algorithm using specific inputs, identify failure cases, and describe what the algorithm does correctly and incorrectly.
criteria: Tests the algorithm with at least three cases including at least one edge or boundary case
Records inputs and outputs systematically
Correctly identifies at least one case where the algorithm fails or produces an unexpected result

nodes.label: Refining and evaluating the algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine an algorithm based on test results and evaluate the refinement, explaining what changed and why it improves the algorithm.
criteria: Makes a specific, justified refinement to the algorithm based on a test failure
Retests with the previously failing case and confirms the refinement resolves it
Evaluates the refined algorithm: states what it now handles correctly and any remaining limitations

descriptors.title: Analysing survey reports
descriptors.description: analyse reports of surveys in digital media and elsewhere for information on how data was obtained to estimate population means and medians

nodes.label: How data is obtained — sampling methods in survey reports
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify from a survey report how data was obtained and explain how the sampling method could affect the representativeness of the sample.
criteria: Identifies the sampling method from the report description
States at least one way the sampling method could limit representativeness or introduce bias
Connects the sampling method to the reliability of the reported statistic

nodes.label: Evaluating statistical claims — means and medians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a claim about a population mean or median by linking it back to how the data was collected and what the data displays show.
criteria: Links a specific statistical claim in a report to the sampling method and data collection process
Assesses whether the claim is adequately supported by the evidence described
Identifies at least one reason why the reported mean or median might not accurately represent the full population

descriptors.title: Sampling methods and representation bias
descriptors.description: analyse how different sampling methods can affect the results of surveys and how choice of representation can be used to support a particular point of view

nodes.label: How sampling method affects results
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how at least two different sampling methods produce different results for the same population and why.
criteria: Correctly describes the mechanism by which each sampling method could introduce bias
Gives a specific example of a population or group that each method would over- or under-represent
Explains why random sampling is generally preferred for population inference

nodes.label: How representation choices support a point of view
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how choices about data visualisation can be used to support a particular viewpoint and assess the strength and fairness of different representations.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific visualisation feature that could create a misleading impression
Explains how changing that feature would affect the viewer's interpretation
Assesses whether the representation fairly represents the data or is designed to support a predetermined conclusion

descriptors.title: Comparative data distributions
descriptors.description: represent the distribution of multiple data sets for numerical variables using comparative representations; compare data distributions with consideration of centre, spread and shape, and the effect of outliers on these measures

nodes.label: Describing distribution shape
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the shape of a data distribution using appropriate terminology (symmetric, positively skewed, negatively skewed, bimodal).
criteria: Correctly identifies symmetric, positively skewed and negatively skewed distributions from graphs
Explains where the 'tail' is in each skewed distribution and which direction it points
Identifies a bimodal distribution and gives a plausible explanation for why two peaks might occur

nodes.label: Comparative representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent two or more data sets using the same comparative display type to allow direct comparison.
criteria: Constructs a correctly labelled comparative representation with aligned scales
Reads at least two summary statistics (e.g. median, range) directly from the representation
Identifies which data set has greater centre and greater spread from the display

nodes.label: Comparing distributions — centre, spread, shape, outliers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare two or more distributions considering centre, spread, shape and the effect of outliers on each measure.
criteria: Compares two distributions using at least three of: centre, spread, shape, outliers
Correctly explains that outliers affect the mean more than the median
States the comparison in contextually meaningful terms (not just as numerical facts)

descriptors.title: Choosing data displays
descriptors.description: choose appropriate forms of display or visualisation for a given type of data; justify selections and interpret displays for a given context

nodes.label: Matching display type to data type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the data type (categorical nominal/ordinal, numerical discrete/continuous) and select an appropriate display type.
criteria: Correctly classifies the data type as categorical (nominal/ordinal) or numerical (discrete/continuous)
Selects an appropriate display type and names it
Justifies the selection with reference to the data type

nodes.label: Justifying and interpreting displays in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can justify a display choice with reference to purpose and audience, and interpret key features of a display in context.
criteria: Justifies a display choice with reference to both data type and purpose/audience
Correctly interprets at least two features of the display in the language of the context
Evaluates whether the display communicates the key message clearly and fairly

descriptors.title: Statistical investigations
descriptors.description: plan and conduct statistical investigations involving the collection and analysis of different kinds of data; report findings and discuss the strength of evidence to support any conclusions

nodes.label: Planning the investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose a statistical question and plan a data collection strategy appropriate to the question, identifying potential sources of bias.
criteria: Poses a statistical question that can be investigated with data
Identifies an appropriate data source (primary or secondary) and justifies the choice
Identifies at least one potential source of bias in the planned data collection

nodes.label: Collecting and analysing data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect or access data appropriate to the investigation and analyse it using suitable representations and summary statistics.
criteria: Collects or accesses data that is relevant to the stated statistical question
Represents the data using an appropriate display type
Calculates at least one relevant summary statistic and states what it means for the investigation

nodes.label: Reporting findings and evaluating evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can report investigation findings and evaluate the strength of evidence supporting their conclusions.
criteria: States at least one finding supported by specific data evidence
Evaluates the strength of that evidence (strong/moderate/weak) and explains why
Identifies at least one limitation of the investigation that affects confidence in the conclusion

descriptors.title: Expand, factorise and simplify
descriptors.description: expand, factorise and simplify expressions and solve equations algebraically, applying exponent laws involving products, quotients and powers of variables, and the distributive property

nodes.label: Exponent laws for algebraic terms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply exponent laws (product, quotient, power of a power) to simplify algebraic expressions involving positive integral exponents.
criteria: Student correctly applies at least two distinct exponent laws to simplify a given algebraic expression
Student can identify which exponent law applies when given a mixed expression

nodes.label: Negative integral exponents
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply exponent laws to expressions involving negative integral exponents and express results with positive exponents.
criteria: Student correctly rewrites expressions with negative exponents in equivalent positive exponent form
Student can derive the negative exponent meaning from the quotient law rather than reciting a rule

nodes.label: Expansion using the distributive property
nodes.checkpoint: Students can expand products of binomials and trinomials using the distributive property, including special products (difference of two squares, perfect square trinomials).
criteria: Student correctly expands a binomial product with no errors including sign handling
Student identifies whether a quadratic expression is a difference of two squares or perfect square trinomial

nodes.label: Factorisation of quadratic expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can factorise monic and non-monic quadratic expressions, including using the completed square form.
criteria: Student correctly factorises a non-monic quadratic expression by an appropriate method
Student converts a monic quadratic to completed square form and explains what each part represents
Student explains why factorisation and expansion are inverse operations

nodes.label: Solving equations algebraically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve equations algebraically by applying exponent laws and factorisation, including quadratic equations.
criteria: Student solves a quadratic equation by factorisation with correct solutions including sign handling
Student verifies solutions by substitution into the original equation

descriptors.title: Linear inequalities and simultaneous equations
descriptors.description: solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables; interpret solutions graphically and communicate solutions in terms of the situation

nodes.label: Solving linear inequalities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a linear inequality in one variable algebraically and represent the solution on a number line.
criteria: Student correctly reverses the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Student represents the solution set correctly on a number line, including open/closed circle distinction

nodes.label: Graphing linear inequalities in two variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can graph the solution region for a linear inequality in two variables in the Cartesian plane and verify a point's membership using substitution.
criteria: Student correctly identifies and shades the solution region for a given linear inequality in two variables
Student verifies whether a specified point satisfies the inequality using substitution

nodes.label: Solving simultaneous linear equations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables using algebraic methods (substitution or elimination).
criteria: Student correctly solves a pair of simultaneous linear equations and verifies the solution in both equations
Student can apply both substitution and elimination, selecting an appropriate method for the given pair

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can formulate a practical problem as simultaneous equations or inequalities, solve it, and communicate the solution in plain language appropriate to the context.
criteria: Student correctly defines variables and formulates simultaneous equations or inequalities from a described context
Student states the solution in terms of the original context using appropriate everyday language
Student identifies whether the solution makes sense within the context's constraints (e.g. integer values, non-negative quantities)

descriptors.title: Exponential functions
descriptors.description: recognise the connection between algebraic and graphical representations of exponential relations and solve related exponential equations, using digital tools where appropriate

nodes.label: Recognising exponential relations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an exponential relation from a table of values by recognising a constant multiplicative ratio between consecutive dependent variable values.
criteria: Student correctly identifies an exponential relation from a table by calculating and confirming the constant multiplicative ratio
Student distinguishes an exponential table from a linear table by identifying the structural difference (ratio vs difference)

nodes.label: Graphical features of exponential functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sketch or interpret the graph of an exponential function, identifying key features including the y-intercept, asymptote, and whether it represents growth or decay.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the y-intercept and horizontal asymptote from an exponential graph or equation
Student states whether an exponential function represents growth or decay and connects this to the base value

nodes.label: Connecting algebraic and graphical representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can move fluently between the algebraic equation and graphical representation of an exponential relation, reading key information from each form.
criteria: Student correctly identifies key graphical features (y-intercept, asymptote, growth/decay) from a given exponential equation
Student writes or identifies the exponential equation corresponding to a given graph

nodes.label: Solving exponential equations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve simple exponential equations by writing both sides in terms of a common base and equating exponents.
criteria: Student correctly rewrites both sides of an exponential equation using a common base
Student solves for the exponent and verifies the solution by substitution

descriptors.title: Model growth and decay
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve applied problems involving growth and decay, including financial contexts; formulate problems, choosing to apply linear, quadratic or exponential models; interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate and modify models as necessary and report assumptions, methods and findings

nodes.label: Selecting the appropriate model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine whether a given growth or decay situation is best modelled as linear, quadratic or exponential by analysing the pattern of change.
criteria: Student correctly classifies a relationship from a table using the appropriate pattern (difference or ratio)
Student justifies the classification by showing the relevant constant pattern in the data

nodes.label: Formulating and applying the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write an equation for a growth or decay model from a described context and use it to answer questions about the situation.
criteria: Student writes a correct exponential model equation identifying initial value and growth/decay factor from a described context
Student uses the equation to calculate a specified value and states it in context-appropriate units

nodes.label: Interpreting and evaluating the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret modelled results in terms of the original situation and evaluate whether the model is appropriate, identifying key assumptions and limitations.
criteria: Student interprets a modelled result in clear context-appropriate language
Student identifies at least one assumption the model makes and explains what would happen if that assumption were violated
Student identifies at least one context in which the model would give unreliable predictions

descriptors.title: Experiment with functions and relations
descriptors.description: experiment with functions and relations using digital tools, making and testing conjectures and generalising emerging patterns

nodes.label: Making and testing conjectures with digital tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a digital graphing tool to explore a function family, formulate a conjecture about an observed pattern, and test it by varying parameters.
criteria: Student states a conjecture as a testable claim (not an observation) about a function family
Student provides evidence from at least two test cases that either supports or contradicts the conjecture

nodes.label: Intersections of functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use digital tools to locate intersection points of two functions and identify coordinate values, including using zoom or bisection to refine approximations.
criteria: Student locates the intersection of two given functions graphically and states the coordinates
Student can refine an approximate intersection point using a zoom or bisection approach

nodes.label: Circles and transformations as relations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can work with the unit circle x² + y² = 1 as a relation, apply transformations, and identify key features of the transformed relation.
criteria: Student correctly graphs the unit circle using a digital tool and explains why it is not a function
Student identifies the effect of a given transformation on the circle's centre and radius

nodes.label: Generalising emerging patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generalise a pattern observed across multiple function experiments into a stated rule or conjecture that applies across a family of cases.
criteria: Student states a generalisation in clear terms that applies to all tested cases
Student tests the generalisation against at least one case not used to form it and reports whether it holds

descriptors.title: Surface area and volume of composite objects
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the surface area and volume of composite objects using appropriate units

nodes.label: Decomposing composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the component solids in a composite object and describe how they combine (addition or subtraction of volumes/surfaces).
criteria: Student correctly identifies the component solids of a given composite object
Student identifies which faces become internal when components join and explains why they are excluded from surface area calculations

nodes.label: Surface area of composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the surface area of a composite object by summing exposed faces of component solids.
criteria: Student correctly calculates the surface area of a composite object with no missing or double-counted faces
Student states the answer in appropriate units

nodes.label: Volume of composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the volume of a composite object by summing or subtracting volumes of component solids.
criteria: Student correctly calculates the volume of a composite object using an appropriate decomposition
Student states the answer in appropriate units and checks reasonableness

nodes.label: Modelling with composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use surface area and volume calculations for composite objects to solve a practical problem, stating assumptions and interpreting results in context.
criteria: Student identifies the composite object structure relevant to the practical problem and performs the correct calculation
Student states the result in context-appropriate terms and identifies at least one assumption made
Student checks whether the result is reasonable given the context

descriptors.title: Logarithmic scales
descriptors.description: interpret and use logarithmic scales in applied contexts involving small and large quantities and change

nodes.label: Order of magnitude and the logarithmic idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that a logarithmic scale is calibrated in orders of magnitude and describe how equal intervals on a log scale represent multiplicative (not additive) steps.
criteria: Student correctly explains what equal intervals represent on a logarithmic scale (multiplicative, not additive steps)
Student reads a value from a base-10 log scale and expresses it as a power of 10

nodes.label: Interpreting logarithmic scales in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and interpret data presented on a logarithmic scale in at least two real-world contexts, explaining what the scale reveals about the data.
criteria: Student correctly reads a value from a logarithmic scale graph and expresses it in appropriate units
Student explains why a logarithmic scale is more appropriate than a linear scale for a given data set

nodes.label: Using logarithmic scales for change and comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use logarithmic scales to compare quantities that span multiple orders of magnitude and interpret what differences between scale values mean.
criteria: Student correctly interprets the multiplicative meaning of a difference between two values on a logarithmic scale
Student compares two quantities on a log scale and expresses the comparison as a ratio

descriptors.title: Pythagoras and trigonometry in practical contexts
descriptors.description: solve practical problems applying Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry of right-angled triangles, including problems involving direction and angles of elevation and depression

nodes.label: Angles of elevation and depression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify angles of elevation and depression in a diagram or described situation and set up the correct right-angled triangle for calculation.
criteria: Student correctly identifies and labels the angle of elevation or depression and the relevant sides in a diagram
Student selects and applies the correct trigonometric ratio to solve for an unknown side or angle

nodes.label: Bearings and direction problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret compass bearings and use trigonometry to solve navigation problems involving direction and distance.
criteria: Student correctly translates a described bearing problem into a labelled right-angled triangle diagram
Student solves for the required distance or angle using appropriate trigonometric ratios

nodes.label: Decomposing 3D problems into 2D
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a right-angled triangle embedded in a 3D situation, extract the relevant 2D problem, and solve it using Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry.
criteria: Student identifies the relevant right-angled triangle within a 3D situation and draws a clear 2D diagram
Student solves the 2D problem correctly and states the answer in context-appropriate terms

descriptors.title: Impact of measurement errors
descriptors.description: identify the impact of measurement errors on the accuracy of results in practical contexts

nodes.label: Sources and types of measurement error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sources of measurement error in a practical context and distinguish between errors arising from the instrument, the method, and the measurer.
criteria: Student identifies at least two sources of measurement error in a described context
Student distinguishes between instrument error, method error, and human error in a given example

nodes.label: Impact of individual measurement errors
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how a measurement error propagates into a calculated result and estimate the size of the impact.
criteria: Student correctly calculates the range of values for a derived quantity given a measurement error margin
Student explains why the impact of a measurement error is larger for some calculations than others

nodes.label: Compounding errors in repeated calculations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how measurement errors compound across repeated or multi-step calculations and describe the effect on accuracy.
criteria: Student explains, with a worked example, how a small error in a single measurement produces a larger error after repeated calculations
Student identifies at least one practical context where accumulated measurement error has meaningful consequences

descriptors.title: Model proportion and scaling
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving proportion and scaling of objects; formulate problems and interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate and modify models as necessary, and report assumptions, methods and findings

nodes.label: Scale factors and conversion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine the scale factor between a model and the actual object, and use it to convert measurements in both directions.
criteria: Student correctly calculates a scale factor from given measurements and applies it to find an unknown dimension
Student explains why area and volume scale differently from linear dimensions

nodes.label: Reading and using scaled plans
